18:37.ar: قَالَ لَهُۥ صَاحِبُهُۥ وَهُوَ يُحَاوِرُهُۥٓ أَكَفَرۡتَ بِٱلَّذِي خَلَقَكَ مِن تُرَابࣲ ثُمَّ مِن نُّطۡفَةࣲ ثُمَّ سَوَّىٰكَ رَجُلࣰ ا
18:37.en: His comrade, when he (thus) spake with him, exclaimed: Disbelievest thou in Him Who created thee of dust, then of a drop (of seed), and then fashioned thee a man

18:38.ar: لَّٰكِنَّا۠ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ رَبِّي وَلَآ أُشۡرِكُ بِرَبِّيٓ أَحَدࣰ ا
18:38.en: But He is Allah, my Lord, and I ascribe unto my Lord no partner

18:39.ar: وَلَوۡلَآ إِذۡ دَخَلۡتَ جَنَّتَكَ قُلۡتَ مَا شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِٱللَّهِۚ إِن تَرَنِ أَنَا۠ أَقَلَّ مِنكَ مَالࣰ ا وَوَلَدࣰ ا
18:39.en: If only, when thou enteredst thy garden, thou hadst said: That which Allah willeth (will come to pass)! There is no strength save in Allah! Though thou seest me as less than thee in wealth and children

18:40.ar: فَعَسَىٰ رَبِّيٓ أَن يُؤۡتِيَنِ خَيۡرࣰ ا مِّن جَنَّتِكَ وَيُرۡسِلَ عَلَيۡهَا حُسۡبَانࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ فَتُصۡبِحَ صَعِيدࣰ ا زَلَقًا
18:40.en: Yet it may be that my Lord will give me better than thy garden, and will send on it a bolt from heaven, and some morning it will be a smooth hillside

18:41.ar: أَوۡ يُصۡبِحَ مَآؤُهَا غَوۡرࣰ ا فَلَن تَسۡتَطِيعَ لَهُۥ طَلَبࣰ ا
18:41.en: Or some morning the water thereof will be lost in the earth so that thou canst not make search for it

18:42.ar: وَأُحِيطَ بِثَمَرِهِۦ فَأَصۡبَحَ يُقَلِّبُ كَفَّيۡهِ عَلَىٰ مَآ أَنفَقَ فِيهَا وَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا وَيَقُولُ يَٰلَيۡتَنِي لَمۡ أُشۡرِكۡ بِرَبِّيٓ أَحَدࣰ ا
18:42.en: And his fruit was beset (with destruction). Then began he to wring his hands for all that he had spent upon it, when (now) it was all ruined on its trellises, and to say: Would that I had ascribed no partner to my Lord

18:43.ar: وَلَمۡ تَكُن لَّهُۥ فِئَةࣱ يَنصُرُونَهُۥ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا كَانَ مُنتَصِرًا
18:43.en: And he had no troop of men to help him as against Allah, nor could he save himself

18:44.ar: هُنَالِكَ ٱلۡوَلَٰيَةُ لِلَّهِ ٱلۡحَقِّۚ هُوَ خَيۡرࣱ ثَوَابࣰ ا وَخَيۡرٌ عُقۡبࣰ ا
18:44.en: In this case is protection only from Allah, the True, He is Best for reward, and best for consequence

18:32.ar: ۞وَٱضۡرِبۡ لَهُم مَّثَلࣰ ا رَّجُلَيۡنِ جَعَلۡنَا لِأَحَدِهِمَا جَنَّتَيۡنِ مِنۡ أَعۡنَٰبࣲ وَحَفَفۡنَٰهُمَا بِنَخۡلࣲ وَجَعَلۡنَا بَيۡنَهُمَا زَرۡعࣰ ا
18:32.en: Coin for them a similitude: Two men, unto one of whom We had assigned two gardens of grapes, and We had surrounded both with date-palms and had put between them tillage

18:33.ar: كِلۡتَا ٱلۡجَنَّتَيۡنِ ءَاتَتۡ أُكُلَهَا وَلَمۡ تَظۡلِم مِّنۡهُ شَيۡـࣰٔ اۚ وَفَجَّرۡنَا خِلَٰلَهُمَا نَهَرࣰ ا
18:33.en: Each of the gardens gave its fruit and withheld naught thereof. And We caused a river to gush forth therein

18:34.ar: وَكَانَ لَهُۥ ثَمَرࣱ فَقَالَ لِصَٰحِبِهِۦ وَهُوَ يُحَاوِرُهُۥٓ أَنَا۠ أَكۡثَرُ مِنكَ مَالࣰ ا وَأَعَزُّ نَفَرࣰ ا
18:34.en: And he had fruit. And he said unto his comrade, when he spake with him: I am more than thee in wealth, and stronger in respect of men

18:35.ar: وَدَخَلَ جَنَّتَهُۥ وَهُوَ ظَالِمࣱ لِّنَفۡسِهِۦ قَالَ مَآ أَظُنُّ أَن تَبِيدَ هَٰذِهِۦٓ أَبَدࣰ ا
18:35.en: And he went into his garden, while he (thus) wronged himself. He said: I think not that all this will ever perish

18:36.ar: وَمَآ أَظُنُّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ قَآئِمَةࣰ وَلَئِن رُّدِدتُّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي لَأَجِدَنَّ خَيۡرࣰ ا مِّنۡهَا مُنقَلَبࣰ ا
18:36.en: I think not that the Hour will ever come, and if indeed I am brought back unto my Lord I surely shall find better than this as a resort

pNFrKAd7RFk.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 8: The Ruin of the Orchard (18:40-44)
pNFrKAd7RFk.one_line: Concluding the story of the two orchards: wealth as a tool not a goal, the illusion of financial security, and dependence on money as hidden shirk.
pNFrKAd7RFk.summary: He closes the parable of the two men and their orchards. The wealthy man misread his money as proof of his worth, felt entitled to it, and so let go of accountability. Before the verses he digresses at length on how wealth should be viewed: money is a means and never the end, children raised in consumer culture learn to equate happiness with money, knowledge must never be pursued for money, and the search for total financial security makes generosity impossible because no amount is ever enough. Insurance is fine in concept as pooled mutual support; the problem is depending on it. He reads the poor friend's words as an explanation of how life works rather than a curse: time humbles every rise, and the one you look down on may outrank you. He leans toward reading the destruction as a scene of the Day of Judgment, linking the dropped fruit and hollow trellises to its imagery. The man's regret 'I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord' shows that relying on wealth is a hidden form of shirk. The fix is to revisit one's dependence often, keep a share of wealth flowing back into the community, and rely on Allah, al-Haqq, whose reward and outcome are best.

outline.heading: Recap: two men, two orchards
outline.gist: Summary of the story so far: the rich man misread his wealth as a sign of personal success rather than an opportunity to do good.

outline.heading: Why abundant wealth pulls people from faith
outline.gist: Wealth carries accountability, so people with a lot of it tend to drift from religion or practise it on their own terms.

outline.heading: Money is a means, not the goal
outline.gist: Human nature wants everything for itself; a Muslim sees money only as a tool for a purpose.

outline.heading: Children, consumerism and 'we can't afford it'
outline.gist: Kids in a consumer culture equate happiness with money; parents should say 'you don't need it now' rather than 'we have no money'.

outline.heading: Knowledge is never pursued for money
outline.gist: Learning, and especially sacred knowledge, is power and character in its own right; money may follow but cannot be its aim.

outline.heading: Wanting more is not wrong
outline.gist: Striving to rise out of poverty or replace what is broken is fine as long as the purpose of wealth is clear.

outline.heading: The two friends' attitudes to money
outline.gist: The poor friend did not hate money; the rich friend thought money made him worth more and gave his word more weight.

outline.heading: The illusion of financial security
outline.gist: Treating money as security makes generosity impossible, since no amount ever covers the next fifty years.

outline.heading: Insurance as an example
outline.gist: Pooled insurance is islamically sound as mutual support; the issue is how companies run it and whether people depend on it instead of Allah.

outline.heading: The friend's advice: say ma sha Allah, la quwwata illa billah
outline.gist: On entering his orchard he should have acknowledged that it exists only by Allah's will and strength.

outline.heading: 'Perhaps my Lord will give me better': the meaning of 'asa
outline.gist: Recitation of the next verses; 'asa signals something very likely, with a sense of hope.

outline.heading: Better in this world or the next?
outline.gist: Scholars differ whether the better garden is in dunya or the Hereafter; he sides with the Hereafter and reads the words as explanation, not a curse.

outline.heading: Husban: a piece of destiny
outline.gist: The word means something decreed to happen; nothing rises in this world except that it is brought down.

outline.heading: Sa'idan zalaqa: barren, slippery ground
outline.gist: Land so flat and pounded that nothing grows, like an old dirt soccer field.

outline.heading: Nothing stays forever
outline.gist: The friend is not vengeful; he explains that wealth passes between people and even a hundred years is not permanence.

outline.heading: The one you look down on will outrank you
outline.gist: People who constantly compare themselves hunt for some field where they are better, and turn depressed or jealous when they find none.

outline.heading: Money is not the measure; assume others are better
outline.gist: Rank is by piety, known only to Allah, so it is safest to assume everyone is better than you and benefit from them.

outline.heading: No one can calculate everything
outline.gist: Thinking one has planned against every risk is impossible; some lose wealth only when resurrected and watch it vanish.

outline.heading: The orchard destroyed: wringing hands over hollow trellises
outline.gist: Turning his palms in regret; khawiyah means hollow from the inside, with only the remnants of the vines left standing.

outline.heading: Not every wealthy disbeliever loses it in this life
outline.gist: Allah never promised that; many tyrants die rich, but all face this loss on the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: Self-worth built on wealth; regret over what he spent
outline.gist: He spent money, effort and hope on the orchard because it was his goal; what is spent for Allah cannot be destroyed.

outline.heading: The root of infaq
outline.gist: Nafaqa and anfaqa share the sense of something being depleted for the sake of something else.

outline.heading: Depending on wealth as hidden shirk
outline.gist: 'I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord': when wealth replaces Allah as one's reliance, it becomes a hidden partner, like showing off in prayer.

outline.heading: Wealth exists to build the community
outline.gist: Saving is fine until it stops you contributing to your community; there is no fixed number, only a clear understanding.

outline.heading: Revise your dependence regularly
outline.gist: Anything could empty a bank account tomorrow; in a paycheque culture a Muslim keeps returning to the question of what he relies on.

outline.heading: The Prophet's own practice versus his teaching on wealth
outline.gist: He kept nothing himself yet told companions to leave their heirs well off and sent back donations that left families with nothing.

outline.heading: No faction to help him
outline.gist: He depended on wealth alone, and when it failed no group or ally could aid him against Allah; change comes to rich and poor alike.

outline.heading: Hunalika al-walayah lillahi al-Haqq
outline.gist: On that day all protection, alliance and aid belong to Allah, al-Haqq, the essence and source of truth.

outline.heading: Best in reward and best in outcome
outline.gist: People chase money for a good end result; relying on Allah gives the better reward and the better end, including after resurrection.

outline.heading: Closing the story
outline.gist: Wrap-up of the parable; the commentary verses that follow will be taken next.

outline.heading: Outro

hadith.gist: It is Allah's way that nothing in the world rises high except that He brings it down.
To leave your heirs well off is better than leaving them poor and begging from people; bequests limited to a third.

18:32.ar: ۞وَٱضۡرِبۡ لَهُم مَّثَلࣰ ا رَّجُلَيۡنِ جَعَلۡنَا لِأَحَدِهِمَا جَنَّتَيۡنِ مِنۡ أَعۡنَٰبࣲ وَحَفَفۡنَٰهُمَا بِنَخۡلࣲ وَجَعَلۡنَا بَيۡنَهُمَا زَرۡعࣰ ا
18:32.en: Coin for them a similitude: Two men, unto one of whom We had assigned two gardens of grapes, and We had surrounded both with date-palms and had put between them tillage

18:33.en: Each of the gardens gave its fruit and withheld naught thereof. And We caused a river to gush forth therein

18:34.ar: وَكَانَ لَهُۥ ثَمَرࣱ فَقَالَ لِصَٰحِبِهِۦ وَهُوَ يُحَاوِرُهُۥٓ أَنَا۠ أَكۡثَرُ مِنكَ مَالࣰ ا وَأَعَزُّ نَفَرࣰ ا
18:34.en: And he had fruit. And he said unto his comrade, when he spake with him: I am more than thee in wealth, and stronger in respect of men

18:35.ar: وَدَخَلَ جَنَّتَهُۥ وَهُوَ ظَالِمࣱ لِّنَفۡسِهِۦ قَالَ مَآ أَظُنُّ أَن تَبِيدَ هَٰذِهِۦٓ أَبَدࣰ ا
18:35.en: And he went into his garden, while he (thus) wronged himself. He said: I think not that all this will ever perish

18:36.ar: وَمَآ أَظُنُّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ قَآئِمَةࣰ وَلَئِن رُّدِدتُّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي لَأَجِدَنَّ خَيۡرࣰ ا مِّنۡهَا مُنقَلَبࣰ ا
18:36.en: I think not that the Hour will ever come, and if indeed I am brought back unto my Lord I surely shall find better than this as a resort

18:28.ar: وَٱصۡبِرۡ نَفۡسَكَ مَعَ ٱلَّذِينَ يَدۡعُونَ رَبَّهُم بِٱلۡغَدَوٰةِ وَٱلۡعَشِيِّ يُرِيدُونَ وَجۡهَهُۥۖ وَلَا تَعۡدُ عَيۡنَاكَ عَنۡهُمۡ تُرِيدُ زِينَةَ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَاۖ وَلَا تُطِعۡ مَنۡ أَغۡفَلۡنَا قَلۡبَهُۥ عَن ذِكۡرِنَا وَٱتَّبَعَ هَوَىٰهُ وَكَانَ أَمۡرُهُۥ فُرُطࣰ ا
18:28.en: Restrain thyself along with those who cry unto their Lord at morn and evening, seeking His Countenance; and let not thine eyes overlook them, desiring the pomp of the life of the world; and obey not him whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who followeth his own lust and whose case hath been abandoned

18:29.ar: وَقُلِ ٱلۡحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكُمۡۖ فَمَن شَآءَ فَلۡيُؤۡمِن وَمَن شَآءَ فَلۡيَكۡفُرۡۚ إِنَّآ أَعۡتَدۡنَا لِلظَّٰلِمِينَ نَارًا أَحَاطَ بِهِمۡ سُرَادِقُهَاۚ وَإِن يَسۡتَغِيثُواْ يُغَاثُواْ بِمَآءࣲ كَٱلۡمُهۡلِ يَشۡوِي ٱلۡوُجُوهَۚ بِئۡسَ ٱلشَّرَابُ وَسَآءَتۡ مُرۡتَفَقًا
18:29.en: Say: (It is) the truth from the Lord of you (all). Then whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve. Lo! We have prepared for disbelievers Fire. Its tent encloseth them. If they ask for showers, they will be showered with water like to molten lead which burneth the faces. Calamitous the drink and ill the resting-place

18:30.ar: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَعَمِلُواْ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ إِنَّا لَا نُضِيعُ أَجۡرَ مَنۡ أَحۡسَنَ عَمَلًا
18:30.en: Lo! as for those who believe and do good works - Lo! We suffer not the reward of one whose work is goodly to be lost

18:31.ar: أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ لَهُمۡ جَنَّٰتُ عَدۡنࣲ تَجۡرِي مِن تَحۡتِهِمُ ٱلۡأَنۡهَٰرُ يُحَلَّوۡنَ فِيهَا مِنۡ أَسَاوِرَ مِن ذَهَبࣲ وَيَلۡبَسُونَ ثِيَابًا خُضۡرࣰ ا مِّن سُندُسࣲ وَإِسۡتَبۡرَقࣲ مُّتَّكِـِٔينَ فِيهَا عَلَى ٱلۡأَرَآئِكِۚ نِعۡمَ ٱلثَّوَابُ وَحَسُنَتۡ مُرۡتَفَقࣰ ا
18:31.en: As for such, theirs will be Gardens of Eden, wherein rivers flow beneath them; therein they will be given armlets of gold and will wear green robes of finest silk and gold embroidery, reclining upon throne therein. Blest the reward, and fair the resting-place

18:9.ar: أَمۡ حَسِبۡتَ أَنَّ أَصۡحَٰبَ ٱلۡكَهۡفِ وَٱلرَّقِيمِ كَانُواْ مِنۡ ءَايَٰتِنَا عَجَبًا
18:9.en: Or deemest thou that the People of the Cave and the Inscription are a wonder among Our portents

59:7.ar: مَّآ أَفَآءَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ رَسُولِهِۦ مِنۡ أَهۡلِ ٱلۡقُرَىٰ فَلِلَّهِ وَلِلرَّسُولِ وَلِذِي ٱلۡقُرۡبَىٰ وَٱلۡيَتَٰمَىٰ وَٱلۡمَسَٰكِينِ وَٱبۡنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِ كَيۡ لَا يَكُونَ دُولَةَۢ بَيۡنَ ٱلۡأَغۡنِيَآءِ مِنكُمۡۚ وَمَآ ءَاتَىٰكُمُ ٱلرَّسُولُ فَخُذُوهُ وَمَا نَهَىٰكُمۡ عَنۡهُ فَٱنتَهُواْۚ وَٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ شَدِيدُ ٱلۡعِقَابِ
59:7.en: That which Allah giveth as spoil unto His messenger from the people of the townships, it is for Allah and His messenger and for the near of kin and the orphans and the needy and the wayfarer, that it become not a commodity between the rich among you. And whatsoever the messenger giveth you, take it. And whatsoever he forbiddeth, abstain (from it). And keep your duty to Allah. Lo! Allah is stern in reprisal

29:46.ar: ۞وَلَا تُجَٰدِلُوٓاْ أَهۡلَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ إِلَّا بِٱلَّتِي هِيَ أَحۡسَنُ إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ مِنۡهُمۡۖ وَقُولُوٓاْ ءَامَنَّا بِٱلَّذِيٓ أُنزِلَ إِلَيۡنَا وَأُنزِلَ إِلَيۡكُمۡ وَإِلَٰهُنَا وَإِلَٰهُكُمۡ وَٰحِدࣱ وَنَحۡنُ لَهُۥ مُسۡلِمُونَ
29:46.en: And argue not with the People of the Scripture unless it be in (a way) that is better, save with such of them as do wrong; and say: We believe in that which hath been revealed unto us and revealed unto you; our Allah and your Allah is One, and unto Him we surrender

VglbpJlnmhI.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 6: The Owner of the Two Gardens
VglbpJlnmhI.one_line: Recap of the cave story's lessons, then the parable of the two gardens: unequal wealth, the purpose of money, and four errors of the wealthy man.
VglbpJlnmhI.summary: He opens on method: stories recur in the Quran because each surah uses the part that serves its theme, and quoting verses out of their context is a major problem for Muslims. He recalls civilisation as a Muslim ideal whose first element is the quality and purpose of the person; without a shared idea, the energy of talented youth scatters. He recaps the cave story and its commentary, stressing companionship and the hadith in which a moment in paradise or hell erases a lifetime's memories. Then he begins the second story. He describes the two gardens in rich detail, with vines, a palm border, crops between and a river, to show that one garden alone would have been more than enough. Why does one man have two and the other none, especially when the poorer man is righteous? This world was not designed for fairness; justice comes in the hereafter, yet Islamic finance aims to keep wealth from circulating only among the rich. Imagining the friends' conversation about success, he identifies four ways the owner wronged himself: treating wealth as permanent security, doubting the Hour so he need not account for his money, hedging his faith like an insurance policy, and feeling entitled to better in the next life.

outline.heading: Why stories recur across surahs
outline.gist: Musa is mentioned more than any prophet because he most resembles the Prophet; each surah tells the part of a story that serves its theme.

outline.heading: His aim: make each surah's theme clear
outline.gist: If the theme is clear, listeners can recover any detail he misses.

outline.heading: Quoting verses out of context
outline.gist: Lifting verses from surahs about something else to prove a ruling is a major problem in how Muslims use the Quran.

outline.heading: Civilisation dropped from our vocabulary
outline.gist: Hadarah was the Prophet's goal; its first element is the quality and purpose of the human being.

outline.heading: Do we qualify as a community?
outline.gist: Numbers and shared beliefs do not make a community without the four basic elements.

outline.heading: The first element: the idea
outline.gist: Without knowing what you stand for, wealth, skills and power do not help and may cause harm.

outline.heading: Energy without a channel
outline.gist: A shared idea is like a tunnel through a mountain; without it gifted youth waste their energy and the same problems recur for a century.

outline.heading: The cave and the tablet
outline.gist: The cave symbolises stepping back to observe reality; the inscription symbolises the agreed charter of values; Allah will do for us what He did for them.

outline.heading: Let the change come through you
outline.gist: Changing the world is beyond us, but we can be the means through which Allah changes it.

outline.heading: Recap of the traits: companionship above all
outline.gist: It was a group, not one person; you need like-minded people around you.

outline.heading: Changing your circle of friends
outline.gist: You may need to distance yourself from some people for Allah's sake; if you find the right ones, stick like glue, even if it is hard.

outline.heading: Recap: say the truth and feel mercy
outline.gist: Present the truth properly, let people choose, and feel mercy rather than hatred for those who refuse.

outline.heading: A single dip in hell or paradise
outline.gist: The most luxurious person dipped once in hell forgets all happiness; the most miserable dipped in paradise forgets all suffering.

outline.heading: Only what is to come matters; read it weekly
outline.gist: Accept hardship and forgive those who refuse; each weekly reading yields something new about building a civilisation.

outline.heading: Recitation: the parable of two men
outline.gist: Recitation of the opening verses of the second story.

outline.heading: Real event or parable?
outline.gist: Scholars differ; with no names, places or times it may be hypothetical; the many meanings of daraba.

outline.heading: Vineyards ringed by palms with a river between
outline.gist: Palm trees protect the vines and repel insects; a river runs between the two gardens.

outline.heading: Both gardens gave their full yield
outline.gist: From a family of farmers, he notes no farmer is ever satisfied, yet these gardens never withheld anything.

outline.heading: Crops between, a river within
outline.gist: Room for vegetables between the trees and water running through: in the Middle East, the king of his land.

outline.heading: He had fruit: the fruits of security
outline.gist: Thamar includes the comfortable life wealth brings, much like our own lifestyle.

outline.heading: Why two gardens for one and none for the other?
outline.gist: The numbers matter in a parable: wealth is not distributed fairly in this world.

outline.heading: This world was not designed to be fair
outline.gist: Justice is served elsewhere; the man with nothing is the righteous one, which makes it seem even more unfair.

outline.heading: Islamic finance keeps wealth circulating
outline.gist: The core principle is that wealth must not circulate only among the rich, so that the poor rise and the rich stay under the law.

outline.heading: When the honest man ends up with less
outline.gist: The hardworking, trustworthy person has less than the one who never cared about ethics.

outline.heading: One garden would have been enough
outline.gist: The detail is there to show he was given far more than he needed; have you felt this unfairness yourself?

outline.heading: Recitation: the conversation and his garden
outline.gist: Recitation of the verses on the two men's dialogue and the owner entering his garden.

outline.heading: Jidal, mira' and hiwar
outline.gist: Argument, pointless disputation and dialogue are different; here it is hiwar, a discussion both think important.

outline.heading: Imagining their conversation about success
outline.gist: Two men in their forties discussing what success is: impact on others, fame or providing for family.

outline.heading: I have more wealth and more men than you
outline.gist: The owner, who cared only for himself, claims he beat his community-minded friend in wealth and status.

outline.heading: What is the point of money?
outline.gist: Is money for showing a bank balance, and is leaving children wealth the measure of success?

outline.heading: The companions' giving
outline.gist: When the Prophet asked for donations, some brought a single date, one gave all he owned and another half.

outline.heading: The friend disagrees
outline.gist: The owner judges by results: more money and social standing, whatever his friend's prayer.

outline.heading: He entered his garden wronging himself
outline.gist: The bracketed phrase is the foundation of the story.

outline.heading: What zulm means
outline.gist: Putting something in the wrong place; Allah owns everything so cannot wrong anyone, yet He defined zulm and forbade it.

outline.heading: Misplacing himself and his money
outline.gist: He wronged himself by seeing himself and his wealth as what they are not.

outline.heading: Four mistakes in his thinking
outline.gist: The four statements reveal four misconceptions about money.

outline.heading: First error: wealth as permanent security
outline.gist: He thought it could never perish; wanting to say 'I will never be poor again' is the wrong reason to earn.

outline.heading: Money is given to do good with
outline.gist: Surplus is for serving Allah and the community; your security rests on Allah, not your account.

outline.heading: Any wealth can vanish
outline.gist: People fall from the richest lists to nothing; no amount brings ultimate security.

outline.heading: An appetite only dust can fill
outline.gist: If money is for security, nothing will ever be enough.

outline.heading: Second error: doubting the Hour
outline.gist: He likes the culture of religion but does not really believe in resurrection.

outline.heading: Never feel secure in anything but Allah
outline.gist: He wronged himself, not his friend; the only constant is Allah, so tie yourself to serving Him.

outline.heading: Wealth's ego boost
outline.gist: It is easy to doubt the Hour sitting comfortably on a throne of wealth.

outline.heading: Denying accountability to justify hoarding
outline.gist: The only way to keep wealth from good is to believe no one will ask about it; many half-believe.

outline.heading: Third error: faith as an insurance policy
outline.gist: One foot in each world: if there is a return, he prayed enough; if not, he enjoyed life.

outline.heading: Fourth error: entitlement
outline.gist: Expecting better in the hereafter; parents hate entitlement in their children, who should feel blessed, not entitled.

outline.heading: Summary of the four problems
outline.gist: Security in money, denying accountability, hedging faith and entitlement: free of these, wealth can build.

18:37.ar: قَالَ لَهُۥ صَاحِبُهُۥ وَهُوَ يُحَاوِرُهُۥٓ أَكَفَرۡتَ بِٱلَّذِي خَلَقَكَ مِن تُرَابࣲ ثُمَّ مِن نُّطۡفَةࣲ ثُمَّ سَوَّىٰكَ رَجُلࣰ ا
18:37.en: His comrade, when he (thus) spake with him, exclaimed: Disbelievest thou in Him Who created thee of dust, then of a drop (of seed), and then fashioned thee a man

18:38.ar: لَّٰكِنَّا۠ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ رَبِّي وَلَآ أُشۡرِكُ بِرَبِّيٓ أَحَدࣰ ا
18:38.en: But He is Allah, my Lord, and I ascribe unto my Lord no partner

18:39.ar: وَلَوۡلَآ إِذۡ دَخَلۡتَ جَنَّتَكَ قُلۡتَ مَا شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِٱللَّهِۚ إِن تَرَنِ أَنَا۠ أَقَلَّ مِنكَ مَالࣰ ا وَوَلَدࣰ ا
18:39.en: If only, when thou enteredst thy garden, thou hadst said: That which Allah willeth (will come to pass)! There is no strength save in Allah! Though thou seest me as less than thee in wealth and children

18:32.ar: ۞وَٱضۡرِبۡ لَهُم مَّثَلࣰ ا رَّجُلَيۡنِ جَعَلۡنَا لِأَحَدِهِمَا جَنَّتَيۡنِ مِنۡ أَعۡنَٰبࣲ وَحَفَفۡنَٰهُمَا بِنَخۡلࣲ وَجَعَلۡنَا بَيۡنَهُمَا زَرۡعࣰ ا
18:32.en: Coin for them a similitude: Two men, unto one of whom We had assigned two gardens of grapes, and We had surrounded both with date-palms and had put between them tillage

18:34.ar: وَكَانَ لَهُۥ ثَمَرࣱ فَقَالَ لِصَٰحِبِهِۦ وَهُوَ يُحَاوِرُهُۥٓ أَنَا۠ أَكۡثَرُ مِنكَ مَالࣰ ا وَأَعَزُّ نَفَرࣰ ا
18:34.en: And he had fruit. And he said unto his comrade, when he spake with him: I am more than thee in wealth, and stronger in respect of men

18:35.ar: وَدَخَلَ جَنَّتَهُۥ وَهُوَ ظَالِمࣱ لِّنَفۡسِهِۦ قَالَ مَآ أَظُنُّ أَن تَبِيدَ هَٰذِهِۦٓ أَبَدࣰ ا
18:35.en: And he went into his garden, while he (thus) wronged himself. He said: I think not that all this will ever perish

18:36.ar: وَمَآ أَظُنُّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ قَآئِمَةࣰ وَلَئِن رُّدِدتُّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي لَأَجِدَنَّ خَيۡرࣰ ا مِّنۡهَا مُنقَلَبࣰ ا
18:36.en: I think not that the Hour will ever come, and if indeed I am brought back unto my Lord I surely shall find better than this as a resort

9:70.ar: أَلَمۡ يَأۡتِهِمۡ نَبَأُ ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبۡلِهِمۡ قَوۡمِ نُوحࣲ وَعَادࣲ وَثَمُودَ وَقَوۡمِ إِبۡرَٰهِيمَ وَأَصۡحَٰبِ مَدۡيَنَ وَٱلۡمُؤۡتَفِكَٰتِۚ أَتَتۡهُمۡ رُسُلُهُم بِٱلۡبَيِّنَٰتِۖ فَمَا كَانَ ٱللَّهُ لِيَظۡلِمَهُمۡ وَلَٰكِن كَانُوٓاْ أَنفُسَهُمۡ يَظۡلِمُونَ
9:70.en: Hath not the fame of those before them reached them - the folk of Noah, A'ad, Thamud, the folk of Abraham, the dwellers of Midian and the disasters (which befell them)? Their messengers (from Allah) came unto them with proofs (of Allah's Sovereignty). So Allah surely wronged them not, but they did wrong themselves

18:4.ar: وَيُنذِرَ ٱلَّذِينَ قَالُواْ ٱتَّخَذَ ٱللَّهُ وَلَدࣰ ا
18:4.en: And to warn those who say: Allah hath chosen a son

4:48.ar: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَغۡفِرُ أَن يُشۡرَكَ بِهِۦ وَيَغۡفِرُ مَا دُونَ ذَٰلِكَ لِمَن يَشَآءُۚ وَمَن يُشۡرِكۡ بِٱللَّهِ فَقَدِ ٱفۡتَرَىٰٓ إِثۡمًا عَظِيمًا
4:48.en: Lo! Allah forgiveth not that a partner should be ascribed unto Him. He forgiveth (all) save that to whom He will. Whoso ascribeth partners to Allah, he hath indeed invented a tremendous sin

49:10.ar: إِنَّمَا ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَ إِخۡوَةࣱ فَأَصۡلِحُواْ بَيۡنَ أَخَوَيۡكُمۡۚ وَٱتَّقُواْ ٱللَّهَ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تُرۡحَمُونَ
49:10.en: The believers are naught else than brothers. Therefore make peace between your brethren and observe your duty to Allah that haply ye may obtain mercy

49:13.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّا خَلَقۡنَٰكُم مِّن ذَكَرࣲ وَأُنثَىٰ وَجَعَلۡنَٰكُمۡ شُعُوبࣰ ا وَقَبَآئِلَ لِتَعَارَفُوٓاْۚ إِنَّ أَكۡرَمَكُمۡ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ أَتۡقَىٰكُمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرࣱ‏
49:13.en: O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct. Lo! Allah is Knower, Aware

TVUH4I1gNhE.speaker: adnan
TVUH4I1gNhE.speaker_note: Seventh session of his own Sunday English tafseer of Al-Kahf; mentions his own university paper on the Farewell Sermon
TVUH4I1gNhE.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 7: The Believer's Reply and the Farewell Sermon
TVUH4I1gNhE.one_line: The two gardens continued: four misconceptions about wealth, the believing friend's reply on creation and tawhid, and saying ma sha Allah; then the Farewell Sermon.
TVUH4I1gNhE.summary: Al-Kahf is read every Friday because it lays out the elements of a society, and its second story is about wealth, which drives nearly everything in the world. Inequality is by design, so people need each other, yet people who accept differences in talent recoil when money is discussed. The owner of the two gardens wronged himself through four misconceptions: wealth as total security, no accountability, faith hedged like insurance, and entitlement, though no one is owed anything, not even existence. The believing friend does not walk away but returns to advise. Asking whether he disbelieves in the One who created him from dust, he points to the origin of life itself, since studying creation cements faith. These errors amount to losing faith, and tawhid matters because people who cannot become gods try to make God smaller so they can write their own rules. The friend's advice is to say ma sha Allah, la quwwata illa billah: a mindset that sees every blessing as Allah's, so one never looks down on those with less. Because the Hajj season has arrived, he closes by reciting his authenticated compilation of the Farewell Sermon: the sanctity of life, wealth and honour, ending pre-Islamic vendettas and usury, the rights of women, equality, and conveying the message.

outline.heading: A surah to read every Friday
outline.gist: A later Meccan surah, uniquely encouraged on Jumu'ah, when the community gathers; its four elements of a civilisation.

outline.heading: The idea comes first
outline.gist: Three teenagers changed a kingdom; Muslims already have the faith and the book, so what remains is to gather and set directions.

outline.heading: Money drives the world
outline.gist: Wars, politics, medicines and weapons all come back to money; the story of two men and two gardens examines it.

outline.heading: Where is the fairness?
outline.gist: Justice was never promised on earth; the story compares a man with excessive wealth and one with much less.

outline.heading: Inequality makes us need each other
outline.gist: Different talents and means push people to cooperate and progress; equal shares would leave no reason to work together.

outline.heading: We change the rules when money comes up
outline.gist: People accept differences in height or skill but step back the moment helping others with money is mentioned.

outline.heading: The questions the story raises
outline.gist: Is wealth a sign of success? How much is enough? Can any amount be immune to loss? What is money for?

outline.heading: Watch how each man views wealth
outline.gist: The believer also wants wealth and works for it, but accepts not having it now.

outline.heading: A conversation about success
outline.gist: Telling a friend 'I have more money and more men' only makes sense if they were debating what success means.

outline.heading: Two views of money
outline.gist: The believer sees wealth as Allah's gift to circulate and create jobs; the owner sees it as proof he is smarter.

outline.heading: He wronged himself by misplacing wealth
outline.gist: The longest commentary in the surah; his friend was not hurt, but he put wealth in the wrong place in his own life.

outline.heading: First misconception: wealth as security
outline.gist: Peace of mind comes from understanding Allah, not from money in the bank.

outline.heading: Second: no accountability
outline.gist: Whatever Allah gives, He asks what you did with it; almost no one has ever refused money.

outline.heading: Third: hedging his faith
outline.gist: If there is a Day, he prayed; if not, he enjoyed his orchards.

outline.heading: Would you still serve Allah when broke?
outline.gist: Serving Allah is easy when things go well; life will not stay this way, so test your faith now.

outline.heading: Fourth: entitlement
outline.gist: Parents hate nothing more than entitlement in their children, hence their stories of hardship.

outline.heading: No one owes you anything
outline.gist: Every good thing is a bonus to be grateful for.

outline.heading: Consciousness itself is an unearned gift
outline.gist: You did not ask for or earn your existence; even those who suffer hate their circumstances, not being someone.

outline.heading: Life itself demands gratitude
outline.gist: We cannot imagine not existing and fear it; everything after the gift of life is extra.

outline.heading: Check yourself for the four
outline.gist: Do we seek security in money, ignore accountability, hedge faith or feel entitled? These lead to downfall.

outline.heading: The friend returns to advise
outline.gist: A good Muslim does not cut off an arrogant friend but comes back to help him; recitation of the friend's reply.

outline.heading: Hiwar, jidal and mira'
outline.gist: Dialogue on important matters, debate to prove a point, and pointless disputation.

outline.heading: Pointless arguments
outline.gist: Talking about personal matters is fine, but fighting over whether Kobe or Jordan was greatest is a waste.

outline.heading: Do you disbelieve in your Creator?
outline.gist: Created from dust, then a drop, then fashioned into a man; the four misconceptions lead toward disbelief.

outline.heading: Security in wealth denies faith in Him
outline.gist: He gave and can take away; entitlement treats Allah as owing us, when we can never repay Him.

outline.heading: Why 'from dust'?
outline.gist: The man was not Adam, so the friend points to the origin of human creation, not mere birth.

outline.heading: From the soil of a young planet
outline.gist: Life emerged from the earth's elements over vast time; grasping that complexity is a different argument from 'you were born'.

outline.heading: Studying creation cements faith
outline.gist: Only humans look up at the stars and question their existence; no lion has a midlife crisis.

outline.heading: Time is relative
outline.gist: You return to dust faster than you came from it; millions of years are nothing to Allah.

outline.heading: Fashioned in balance
outline.gist: Sawwaka: your body functions perfectly; how could you lose faith?

outline.heading: I will not associate anyone with my Lord
outline.gist: Why tawhid is the one thing Allah will not forgive, rather than murder or theft.

outline.heading: Making God more like us
outline.gist: Humans want to be like gods; failing that, they give God partners or children to level the field.

outline.heading: A lesser god lets us write our own rules
outline.gist: If God is not all-knowing, His commands become guidelines and halal and haram become preferences.

outline.heading: Tawhid is belief in His perfection
outline.gist: All religions once shared the same values; tawhid means taking His values as absolute, including on money.

outline.heading: Wealth is a means, and the hardest test
outline.gist: After the Prophet died, people withheld zakat; everything is fine until money or life is at stake.

outline.heading: Abu Lahab chose his business
outline.gist: He had every reason to accept Islam but saw tawhid as a threat to his trade.

outline.heading: Recitation of the next verse
outline.gist: Recitation of the verse on what he should have said on entering his garden.

outline.heading: It would have been better
outline.gist: Lawla here means it would have been better had you said this when you entered.

outline.heading: Ma sha Allah, la quwwata illa billah
outline.gist: Awe at Allah's will and the admission that there was no power to gain it except through Him, even if you see me as having less.

outline.heading: Wealth as opportunity and accountability
outline.gist: Better still, he should never have seen others' poverty as failure.

outline.heading: Say it in your happiest moments
outline.gist: When you hear your family downstairs and feel content, attribute it to Allah right away.

outline.heading: A mindset, not a cultural phrase
outline.gist: Seeing blessings as Allah's means never looking down on those who have less.

outline.heading: Why the Farewell Sermon now
outline.gist: Each Hajj season he recites the sermon from a paper he wrote authenticating its narrations; the Prophet delivered it in parts several times, four months before he died.

outline.heading: From Safa to a hundred thousand
outline.gist: Twenty years after being silenced on Safa, the Prophet addressed a hundred thousand followers.

outline.heading: He never saw the golden age
outline.gist: Within decades Islam spanned from Mauritania to China, but he left principles rather than seeing the fruit.

outline.heading: Opening: praise and 'I may not meet you again'
outline.gist: He began with gratitude to Allah, as the story teaches, and asked people to listen.

outline.heading: What day, month and land is this?
outline.gist: Repeated rhetorical questions held attention; criers on horseback relayed each paragraph to the crowd.

outline.heading: Life and wealth are more sacred than all of it
outline.gist: A Muslim's blood and property outrank the sacred day, month and land combined.

outline.heading: No harm even within families
outline.gist: No harm from father to son; believers are brothers; he called Allah to witness that he had conveyed it.

outline.heading: Jahiliyyah under my feet

QOBsNyPURHE.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 10: The Book That Leaves Nothing Out and Iblis's Entitlement (18:49-51)
QOBsNyPURHE.one_line: The record that omits nothing, being questioned about every blessing, generosity as the remedy, and Iblis's entitlement as the model of misreading what Allah gives.
QOBsNyPURHE.summary: He recaps the surah's four building blocks of a civilisation, stressing that without the guiding idea, wealth, knowledge and power are energy wasted in an endless loop. On the Day of Judgment every degree, title and network is stripped away and only character, belief and deeds remain, like the base layer of a cake. He then explains the presented book: the criminals, those who broke the norms of goodness, are physically shaken, cry out at a record that misses no small or large deed, and find all of it present, yet Allah wrongs no one. Much of that record will concern wealth they no longer hold, as the Prophet's tears over a simple meal with Abu Bakr and Umar showed. The way out is generosity without counting, giving a fixed share for Allah, and remembering that unequal distribution means surplus wealth is for the community. The story of Iblis comes here because he felt entitled to his rank and refused to honour Adam; people who treat wealth as proof of their worth repeat his mistake. Those who think like him are the real enemy. Allah did not make them witnesses to creation, so no one is entitled to anything. What lasts is what is given away.

outline.gist: An ethical term for those who steal, kill and wrong others, whatever their religion.

outline.gist: They blame the book, which leaves out nothing small or large, every glance and smile counted like a census.

outline.gist: They find all they did before them, and Allah oppresses no one.

outline.heading: Much of the book concerns wealth
outline.gist: Picturing that page is the best way to straighten your path; wealth means every material blessing, not just cash.

outline.heading: The Prophet's tears over a simple meal
outline.gist: Driven out by hunger with Abu Bakr and Umar, fed by a generous companion, he wept recalling that we will be asked about every blessing.

outline.heading: Questioned about wealth you no longer hold
outline.gist: On that day you own nothing yet must answer for every coin; seeing this shifts how one views money without making it negative.

outline.heading: Wealth as gift and responsibility
outline.gist: It will be numbered: how much, where it went, and whether others needed it more.

outline.heading: Generosity without counting
outline.gist: The Prophet told one of his family not to count her charity lest Allah count against her; give a set share with an open heart.

outline.heading: Generosity covers every flaw
outline.gist: A generous person's faults are forgotten, but a heart clinging to money as security cannot be generous.

outline.heading: Unequal distribution means surplus is for others
outline.gist: Had wealth been given equally, managing your own would suffice; because it was not, everything beyond need is for the community.

outline.heading: A note on how the mushaf writes 'mal hadha'
outline.gist: The separated spelling may reflect how the companions wrote rather than a hidden meaning; he does not claim to know.

outline.heading: Iblis refuses to prostrate
outline.gist: Recitation; the prostration was respect for Adam's superior creation, which the angels accepted at once.

outline.heading: Kana min al-jinn; fasaqa: breaking off the path
outline.gist: A jinn raised to the angels' company; fisq is breaking away, like a seedling bursting from its seed.

outline.heading: Iblis's entitlement and ours
outline.gist: He felt his worship earned him rank over someone who had done nothing; self-made wealthy people can fall into the same trap.

outline.heading: We deserve nothing; Allah cannot wrong what He owns
outline.gist: If Allah punished all His creation He would not be wronging them, since everything already belongs to Him.

outline.heading: Taking Iblis and his offspring as allies
outline.gist: The offspring are those who think like him, treating blessings as status; that way of thinking is the true enemy.

outline.heading: Why the illusion is stronger today
outline.gist: A bank balance or company valuation gives a security the companions' crops never did, and everything is now measured in money.

outline.heading: Is Iblis the father of the jinn?
outline.gist: A question from the audience; there is no evidence for it and our knowledge of the jinn is very limited.

outline.heading: Turn every blessing into responsibility
outline.gist: Never let what Allah sends cloud your view of yourself or others; see it as a duty to give more.

outline.heading: Not witnesses to creation, not Allah's helpers
outline.gist: They saw neither the heavens and earth nor their own creation, so no one is entitled; Allah takes no misleaders as supporters.

outline.heading: All of it remains except its shoulder
outline.gist: Aisha gave away a slaughtered sheep but its shoulder; the Prophet said what was given is what remains.

outline.heading: Outro

18:22.en: (Some) will say: They were three, their dog the fourth, and (some) say: Five, their dog the sixth, guessing at random; and (some) say: Seven, and their dog the eighth. Say (O Muhammad): My Lord is Best Aware of their number. None knoweth them save a few. So contend not concerning them except with an outward contending, and ask not any of them to pronounce concerning them

18:23.ar: وَلَا تَقُولَنَّ لِشَاْيۡءٍ إِنِّي فَاعِلࣱ ذَٰلِكَ غَدًا

SeHnJ-O9VVA.one_line: Five lessons from the commentary verses after the cave story: ignore trivia, plan by Allah's will, do your part, recite His words, and keep righteous company.
SeHnJ-O9VVA.summary: He reminds the audience that Al-Kahf's four unique stories teach the four elements of a sustainable civilisation: the idea, wealth, knowledge and power, with the idea first, since knowledge, money and status are wasted without clear values. He then draws five concepts from verses 22 to 28. First, the debate over how many sleepers there were is a distraction; the Quran left it out deliberately, and Muslims likewise fuss over appearances while Allah looks at hearts. Do not argue or ask about what is unclear and useless. Second, saying in sha Allah means asking whether a plan is something Allah wills and would be pleased with; remember Him when you forget, and ask Him to guide you to something closer to rashad, meaning pleasing Him and succeeding. Third, Allah knows and controls everything, down to 300 solar years being 309 lunar ones, so do your part, fill a gap, and never give up hope; a few teenagers changed a kingdom. Fourth, keep reciting His words, whose principles never change, and rely on nothing else. Fifth, patiently hold on to like-minded friends who call on their Lord, even if they seem less fun, and do not follow the heedless. He ends with a story of a companion who won back a friend with a gentle letter.

outline.gist: Verses 22 to 31 comment on the story and are among the richest commentaries in the Quran; a recitation note on the first verse.

outline.heading: The theme: four elements of a civilisation
outline.gist: Al-Kahf tells four stories found nowhere else in the Quran, each on one element a prosperous society needs.

outline.heading: Why recite it weekly: the idea comes first
outline.gist: Power, knowledge, wealth and, first of all, the idea: clear values and purpose without which everything else is lost.

outline.heading: Even an individual is wasted without the idea
outline.gist: The cave youth wrote down what they stood for; giving children education, jobs and connections means nothing without a mindset.

outline.heading: Most people live without a cause
outline.gist: Most people, Muslims included, live with no purpose; the cave youth decided to stand for something.

outline.heading: First comment: their number is a distraction
outline.gist: Three and a dog, five, seven: guessing in the dark about something irrelevant to the story's lesson.

outline.heading: The rabbis' question and the debated number
outline.gist: Quraysh asked the Prophet questions from Jewish scholars, who themselves disputed the number; the Quran reproduced their debate exactly.

outline.heading: Recap: a few youths changed a kingdom
outline.gist: They took a stand in a corrupt kingdom; after 300 years their written principles spread and the kingdom turned to Allah.

outline.heading: Allah bends physical laws for those who stand
outline.gist: Their rare stand was met with a rare miracle, yet people spend hours on the number and the dog.

outline.heading: Allah looks at hearts, not appearances
outline.gist: We fuss about outward details and neglect intentions, thoughts and ambitions, which are His first concern.

outline.heading: Do not argue over what is unclear
outline.gist: Mira' is debating what is doubtful in its essence; argue a clear issue, but leave unclear ones at what Allah said.

outline.heading: Do not ask anyone about it
outline.gist: Ask only what you need to function as a Muslim; the mind has limited space, so do not fill it with clutter.

outline.heading: End of the first comment; recitation of the next verses
outline.gist: Focus on what matters in the surah; recitation of the verses on saying in sha Allah.

outline.heading: Second comment: in sha Allah is a question
outline.gist: Before declaring what you will do tomorrow, ask whether it is something Allah wills and wants for you.

outline.heading: No one says in sha Allah for a sin
outline.gist: Even the simple meaning implies the plan must be something Allah would be pleased with.

outline.heading: Testing your ambitions
outline.gist: Can you say in sha Allah about becoming an athlete or artist? Only if it serves Allah; he jokes about teaching being unrewarding.

outline.heading: Remember your Lord when you forget
outline.gist: If a plan leaves Allah out, step back; the cave youth reassessed when their reality changed and retreated to the cave.

outline.heading: A golden ticket for every decision
outline.gist: Asking whether Allah would be pleased with even weekend plans keeps you from getting lost.

outline.heading: Closer to rashad
outline.gist: 'Asa expresses hope; rashad means success in this life that continues into the next.

outline.heading: Two criteria: pleasing Allah and succeeding
outline.gist: Allah does not want failing plans; intend success for His sake and ask Him to improve your human, flawed plan.

outline.heading: A unique dua and the pursuit of excellence
outline.gist: No other dua is like it; everything can be done better, which is what ihsan is.

outline.heading: Recap of the first two comments; recitation
outline.gist: Be substantial, plan for Allah and keep asking Him to refine the plan; recitation of the verses on their 309 years.

outline.heading: Third comment: Allah knows; do your part
outline.gist: Your control is near zero; find the gap that needs filling and spend your short life filling it.

outline.heading: What can three teenagers do?
outline.gist: The youth thought their effort limited; Allah showed them a whole kingdom turned Muslim through them.

outline.heading: 300 years, adding nine
outline.gist: He has the audience calculate: 11 days a year over 300 years is about nine years, the difference between solar and lunar calendars.

outline.heading: He knows the unseen; how well He sees and hears
outline.gist: Allah knows the measurable and the unmeasurable; the verse uses the Arabic form of wonder to magnify Himself.

outline.heading: No protector besides Him: never give up hope
outline.gist: Whom are you trying to impress if not Him? Know reality to plan, but it has nothing to do with doing your part.

outline.heading: Fourth comment: recite, His words never change
outline.gist: Tilawah of what was revealed; the principles in His words are not subject to time or place.

outline.heading: The unchanging law brings peace of mind
outline.gist: Stand for Allah and He stands by you; do your part and leave the results to Him.

outline.heading: Nothing to lean on besides Him
outline.gist: Multahad is something to put your back against; others' words may hold wisdom, but only His are reliable.

outline.heading: How the four concepts connect; learning takes time
outline.gist: Once you accept the first three you will ask for principles; the youth sought scholars of the book in their time.

outline.heading: Break the ceiling on your potential
outline.gist: If Allah is limitless and you work within His will, do not limit yourself.

outline.heading: Recitation of the fifth verse
outline.gist: Recitation of the verse that ties the commentary together.

outline.heading: Fifth comment: patience means it will be hard
outline.gist: Wasbir nafsak: fill yourself with perseverance, because the command is heavy.

outline.heading: Seeking His face
outline.gist: The phrase took on its meaning in Islam, since seeing Allah is the greatest reward of paradise.

outline.heading: Stay with the like-minded, even if less fun
outline.gist: Devout people are often not the coolest company; the youth succeeded because they were a group, unlike a man who stood alone.

outline.heading: Do not let your eyes pass beyond them
outline.gist: If you found someone who loves Allah as you do, do not even glance elsewhere.

outline.heading: Righteous friends need not be rare
outline.gist: They would be common if such people stuck together and stopped fighting over trivia; the grass always looks greener.

outline.heading: Not seeking the adornment of this life
outline.gist: Righteous company can still be fun and adventurous; there are no perfect friends, so do not leave them over flaws.

outline.heading: Do not follow the heedless
outline.gist: Youth tends to indifference; the cave youth were young but cared, so do not befriend or follow those who do not.

outline.heading: A life scattered like a broken string of beads
outline.gist: Furut: following desires leaves a life without structure or reward, like wealth and knowledge without the idea.

outline.heading: You are on your friend's religion
outline.gist: Choose and hold on to friends who bring you closer to Allah; one of the most precious things in life.

outline.heading: The letter that brought a friend back
outline.gist: A companion, told his friend had taken to drink, wrote him a verse on Allah forgiving sins and accepting repentance; the man repented.

0SDLl4PBsAI.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 13: Musa Sets Out, Theory Meets Practice (18:60-62)
0SDLl4PBsAI.one_line: Opening the story of Musa and al-Khidr: knowledge as a tool, the gap between theory and practice, and the junction of the two seas as their meeting point.
0SDLl4PBsAI.summary: He opens the third story, on knowledge, with long background. Stories in the Quran begin mid-event, so context is essential. Musa, asked who was most knowledgeable, honestly said himself; prophets never tied knowledge to rank, since only piety makes one better and only Allah knows it. Like ideas and wealth, knowledge is a tool that can raise or ruin, as the hadith of the scholar thrown first into the Fire shows, and the Quran never splits knowledge into worldly and religious. His central point: Musa had so far only taught theory, as Makkah was theory and Madinah practice. Practice is a different skill, as when a janitor saved a patient he could not help as a new doctor. Many speakers and movements are cut off from reality; da'wah today means functioning communities, not debates. A messy masjid full of youth is what practice looks like. Rulings shaped by lived reality, such as Ibn Hazm in Andalusia permitting music, take courage, while declaring everything haram is easy. Musa brings his student to learn alongside him, and his 'I will not quit until I reach' is a slogan for life. The junction of the two seas and the dead fish coming alive symbolise theory and practice meeting; young Yusha' missing the sign shows the young need elders to model practice.

outline.heading: Recap: idea and wealth

outline.heading: The third story: often misused
outline.gist: A highly symbolic story that will take the longest and is commonly misunderstood.

outline.heading: Quranic stories need background
outline.gist: Stories start halfway through events; without context, as with Surat al-Tawbah, passages are hard to understand.

outline.heading: Musa and a story told only here

outline.heading: 'Who is most knowledgeable?' An honest answer
outline.gist: Musa said himself, not from arrogance, since prophets did not tie knowledge to status; only piety ranks people and only Allah knows it.

outline.heading: Knowledge, like ideas and wealth, cuts both ways
outline.gist: Good ideas build civilisations and bad ones cause world wars; knowledge can deepen you or make you arrogant.

outline.heading: The scholar who fuels the Fire first
outline.gist: Knowing more does not make you better; one who learned to be called a scholar is among the first thrown into Hell.

outline.heading: The four elements are tools
outline.gist: That is why each story is followed by commentary warning of misuse.

outline.heading: No split between worldly and religious knowledge
outline.gist: The Quran treats all true knowledge as one, never praises ignorance, and wants faith grounded in knowledge.

outline.heading: Musa had only preached so far
outline.gist: The question came just after crossing the sea; his message had been taught but never practised.

outline.heading: Theory versus practice in any field
outline.gist: Knowing a formula or what trade means is not solving problems or succeeding in business.

outline.heading: The janitor and the cardiac arrest
outline.gist: As a new doctor on call he could not find the crash cart; a janitor who knew the ward saved the patient.

outline.heading: Rulings disconnected from reality
outline.gist: A mufti who has never been on the ground gives answers that are dead before they are born.

outline.heading: Seeing the bigger picture takes practice
outline.gist: Islam understood in compartments by those who only teach in the masjid stays partial.

outline.heading: Makkah was theory, Madinah was practice
outline.gist: Could Islam make emigrants and Ansar share homes, or unite tribes at war for a century? Madinah proved it.

outline.heading: A million talkers, too few doers
outline.gist: One speaker is enough; the need is people practising. Many scholars and movements have a rosy, disconnected view.

outline.heading: Musa wanted to learn, not defend himself
outline.gist: Told someone knew more, he was not offended and asked at once where to find him.

outline.heading: Da'wah is functioning communities, not debates
outline.gist: Strong families, engaged youth and no neglected Muslim draw people to Islam in crowds; talk is cheap.

outline.heading: The messy masjid is what practice looks like
outline.gist: Complaints about loud youth miss the point; the Prophet dealt with a man urinating in the masjid.

outline.heading: Parents and scholars who haven't seen it
outline.gist: Working with youth since his own youth taught him how different reality is from what most assume.

outline.heading: Respect for knowledge without switching off your mind
outline.gist: Musa became deeply humble before the teacher yet still objected each time, which was right.

outline.heading: Knowing patience versus living grief
outline.gist: Knowing how to respond to loss or treat your wife is different from doing it; lectures run their course.

outline.heading: Shared values are worthless unpractised
outline.gist: All civilisations share values; information is free online, even how to build nuclear power, but doing is rare.

outline.heading: Literal text versus its purpose
outline.gist: Understanding why a text exists lets you serve its aim in new circumstances, which takes depth and courage.

outline.heading: Music as an example: rulings shaped by reality
outline.gist: Middle Eastern scholars forbade it while Ibn Hazm and Maliki scholars in Andalusia, living with it, permitted instruments.

outline.heading: Courage versus calling everything haram
outline.gist: Theology is fixed, rulings adapt within limits; blanket bans are easy, popular and leave youth lost and percentages falling.

outline.heading: Musa brings his student along
outline.gist: He let Yusha' see him learn, as his own teachers took him to their teachers; don't hide the humility of learning.

outline.heading: Take your children with you
outline.gist: Children learn manners by watching you among people, not from lectures at home or school theory.

outline.heading: 'I will not quit until I reach'
outline.gist: Musa's resolve as a slogan worth putting on your wall.

outline.heading: Majma' al-bahrayn: where theory and practice meet
outline.gist: Its location doesn't matter; it is symbolic, and the dead coming to life is knowledge made alive, as the Prophet's character was the Quran.

outline.heading: Ramadan as practice
outline.gist: Knowledge is easy to gather; the same fasting questions every year show the gap, while Ramadan forces practice.

outline.heading: Huquba: willing to spend decades
outline.gist: He would spend a lifetime to learn what he lacked: knowledge needed for his role, not every detail of botany.

outline.heading: The fish comes alive and slips into the sea
outline.gist: They reached the junction and passed it; Yusha' saw the fish leap into the water while Musa slept, and forgot.

outline.heading: The young need elders to make the connection
outline.gist: Yusha' missed the sign; youth need to see theory practised by older people.

outline.heading: His uncle kissing his aunt's hand
outline.gist: Seeing a respected sixty-year-old kiss his elderly aunt's hand taught him respect in a way lectures never had.

outline.heading: 'Bring our lunch, we are worn out'
outline.gist: Hunger after passing the junction reminds Yusha'; summary of the theory-practice symbolism.

kzAZIPis1xE.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 5: Speak the Truth, Then Let People Choose
kzAZIPis1xE.one_line: Recap of the cave commentary's five traits, then verses 29-31: proclaim the truth from your Lord without compulsion, and trust the promised outcome.
kzAZIPis1xE.summary: He asks why two billion Muslims, and a local community of thousands, have so little impact, and answers that they lack the first element of Al-Kahf: a clear idea of what they stand for, held by like-minded people. A few youths changed a kingdom, so every effort ripples outward if people organise around shared principles. He recaps the five traits from the previous verses: substance over appearances, as in money spent on decorating mosques or merely sending children to school; plans tied to Allah's will; trust that all is in His hands, with no worry that paralyses; the Quran as the source of principles; and like-minded companions, at least three. Verse 29 gives the sixth: say the truth that comes from your Lord, everywhere. Al-Haqq is Allah's name and the basis of creation, and nothing outranks doing what is right, even when fear, status or unpopularity pushes otherwise, as when Palestine falls out of fashion. Then let people choose: Islam has no interest in compulsion, since forcing belief only produces hypocrites. Before blaming the world, ask whether Muslims have presented Islam at all. The vivid punishment and reward in verses 29 to 31 should turn anger at rejection into mercy and keep believers working without despair.

outline.heading: Recap: four unique stories, four elements
outline.gist: The idea, wealth, knowledge and power, each in a story found only in Al-Kahf; next comes the story of the two gardens.

outline.heading: Without the idea, nothing else works
outline.gist: Wealth, knowledge and power achieve nothing unless channelled by shared values.

outline.heading: Why Muslim numbers bring no impact
outline.gist: Two billion Muslims and tens of thousands locally, yet little effect, because the idea is unclear to us.

outline.heading: The cave youth knew what they stood for
outline.gist: They wrote their principles down; our problem is not the religion but our lack of clarity on what we want.

outline.heading: The ripple effect of doing your part
outline.gist: Spreading a message or helping the uneducated may seem futile, but its effect will appear.

outline.heading: Sit with like-minded people and ask questions
outline.gist: Gather people with similar goals to ask what needs fixing and how to organise; the youths met by chance and changed a society.

outline.heading: Different perspectives and circles of influence
outline.gist: Start with yourself and family, then connect with others into a network; teenagers did this, so do not call yourself limited.

outline.heading: First trait: substance over appearances
outline.gist: We fuss over youths' hats and haircuts and pour money into mosque decor, while the Prophet changed the world from a mosque roofed with palm leaves.

outline.heading: Educating children versus sending them to school
outline.gist: Schooling is not the same as raising people with clarity of purpose.

outline.heading: Second trait: decisions under Allah's will
outline.gist: Not just saying in sha Allah but asking whether the plan is Allah's will or mine, and seeking something closer to right guidance.

outline.heading: Third trait: it is all in His hands
outline.gist: He knew the exact years they slept and sees and hears all, however dark things look.

outline.heading: Worry that plans, not worry that paralyses
outline.gist: Healthy concern helps planning; despair that nothing can change stops you doing your job.

outline.heading: Fourth trait: take your principles from the Quran
outline.gist: Recite what was revealed to find the guidance for your way of life.

outline.heading: Fifth trait: hold on to the like-minded
outline.gist: Persevere with those who call on their Lord, even if they are not the coolest, and do not follow the heedless.

outline.heading: Enough such people are already here
outline.gist: People in this room share the same aspirations; the question is bringing in the other elements.

outline.heading: Three is the smallest group
outline.gist: The sleepers' smallest suggested number was three, the smallest jama'ah; find a group that agrees on fundamentals.

outline.heading: Recitation of verse 29
outline.gist: Recitation and pronunciation notes on the sixth commentary verse.

outline.heading: Sixth trait: the narrative to present
outline.gist: Two readings: say 'the truth is from your Lord', or speak the truth whose source is your Lord.

outline.heading: Speak of the truth in every setting
outline.gist: Explain what righteousness is and what comes from Allah at every opportunity.

outline.heading: Al-Haqq: Allah's name and the basis of creation
outline.gist: Allah created the heavens and earth with truth; anything ranked above doing right is a cancer in a community.

outline.heading: Truth before personal agendas
outline.gist: Do not spread your own agenda or overlook truths that do not suit you; it is harder than it sounds.

outline.heading: Fear and the non-negotiables
outline.gist: Fear of physical, financial or social harm silences people; know what can never be compromised, such as justice and equality.

outline.heading: Silent when the truth is unpopular
outline.gist: Palestine, occupied for seventy years, is spoken of only when world media allow it; others harm the cause by misunderstanding the truth.

outline.heading: People grow bored of causes
outline.gist: Issues get pushed to the back page, but substance, reliance on Allah and good company keep you on the truth.

outline.heading: Whoever wills, let him believe
outline.gist: After presenting the truth, the choice is theirs, though not without consequences.

outline.heading: Why force someone onto your team?
outline.gist: A player who does not believe in the team is useless; Allah holds people accountable, not us.

outline.heading: Compulsion only creates hypocrites
outline.gist: Muslims have no interest in forcing religion; hypocrisy is the worst outcome, while clear difference allows coexistence.

outline.heading: Have we presented the truth before blaming the world?
outline.gist: Allah gave people free will; our part is to establish, discuss and display the truth, then let people choose.

outline.heading: We read this every week
outline.gist: Do not leave the presentation of Islam to non-Muslims with their own agendas; ask why we are not doing our own part.

outline.heading: Some accept late
outline.gist: We cannot even care for our own youth; many Meccans accepted Islam only after years and then had great impact.

outline.heading: A fire walled like a fortress
outline.gist: Suradiq: the multi-layered walls of a fort, so the wrongdoers have nowhere to go.

outline.heading: Respond to rejection with mercy
outline.gist: Someone refusing is in danger he does not see; question your own presentation, as the Prophet held people back from the fire like moths.

outline.heading: The Prophet's grief at Badr
outline.gist: Addressing the fallen of Quraysh, he grieved that he could not save them.

outline.heading: Take it easy: results are not your burden
outline.gist: If they refuse, the scale of the reward and punishment removes your agony; their drink will be like molten metal.

outline.heading: The worst resting place; recitation of 30-31
outline.gist: Murtafaq is a place to recline on your elbows; then recitation of the reward verses.

outline.heading: No reward of the doers of good is lost
outline.gist: Those who believe and do the deeds they were created for; the plan and its steps lead here.

outline.heading: Unrewarding work is all recorded
outline.gist: Even after decades without visible change, nothing you did is lost.

outline.heading: Gardens, gold and green silk
outline.gist: Rivers beneath them, bracelets of gold, garments of silk, reclining on couches: how could you feel despair working toward this?

outline.heading: Never stop doing what is right
outline.gist: He asks forgiveness if he could not convey the beauty, and urges people to continue.

outline.heading: The cave section is the longest for a reason
outline.gist: Establishing the idea, principles, companions and plan is the most important step; without it wealth, knowledge and power mean nothing.

outline.heading: Outro

kPfMWgYAOyI.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Kahf, Session 14: Mercy with Knowledge, and Patience Needs Understanding (18:63-70)
kPfMWgYAOyI.one_line: Yusha' and the forgotten fish, blaming Shaytan, why knowledge needs mercy, Musa's humble request, and why no one can be patient with what they don't understand.
kPfMWgYAOyI.summary: Knowledge, he says, enlarges the pot of a person's potential; whether it gets filled is a choice. Young Yusha' says Shaytan made him forget the fish, which is an acknowledgement, not shifting blame, since Shaytan can only whisper; he criticises cultural superstitions about jinn and exorcism. Musa and Yusha' retrace their footsteps and find a servant given mercy from Allah and knowledge from His presence. Knowledge and mercy are paired across the Quran because knowledge without mercy is abused: science is a blessing and a tool, not a goal, and without compassion it builds weapons and military budgets while people starve. The same applies to sending children to university or seeking religious knowledge without guidance. Musa asks humbly to follow and learn rushd, the practical wisdom echoed in the cave youths' prayer. The reply, that he cannot be patient with what he does not fully grasp, is a principle: people cannot commit to what they don't understand, which is why Islam never asks for blind belief. Real knowledge with mercy lets you understand why others act as they do. Youth will not keep chastity or hijab without real understanding, so awareness must rise. Musa promises patience and obedience, and the teacher's one condition is that he ask nothing until told.

outline.heading: Recap: knowledge, the third element
outline.gist: Idea, wealth and now knowledge; this story appears nowhere else in the Quran.

outline.heading: Musa's knowledge had not met reality
outline.gist: He had taught for years under Pharaoh's oppression without any chance to practise; we mostly learn from the Israelites' mistakes.

outline.heading: Knowledge enlarges the pot
outline.gist: Education raises potential; some have big empty pots, others small full ones, and filling it is a choice.

outline.heading: Recap: the junction and the fish
outline.gist: Where theory and practice meet, dead societies and spirits come to life; Yusha' saw it but missed the connection.

outline.heading: Youth need to see values practised
outline.gist: Like a solved example after a formula; academia produces experts who have never applied their knowledge.

outline.heading: Yusha' remembers at the rock
outline.gist: Asked for lunch, he recalls the fish came alive while they rested at the rock and he forgot to say.

outline.heading: 'Only Shaytan made me forget'
outline.gist: Not shifting blame but acknowledging a participant in his own mistake.

outline.heading: Shaytan only whispers
outline.gist: Blaming Shaytan for everything is wrong; he is a declared enemy but you choose whether to accept his suggestion.

outline.heading: Superstition about jinn and exorcism
outline.gist: A woman pouring molten lead around his educated parents' home when he was thirteen; such practices lack evidence and prey on people.

outline.heading: 'It took its way into the sea, amazingly'
outline.gist: The seasoned fish came alive; Musa says that is what they were seeking.

outline.heading: Retracing their footsteps
outline.gist: Qasas: following their own tracks back through unfamiliar land to the exact spot.

outline.heading: A servant given mercy and knowledge
outline.gist: Rahmah min 'indina is something given in measure; 'ilm min ladunna is unmeasured.

outline.heading: Mercy and knowledge paired in the Quran
outline.gist: From 'mercy to the worlds' to 'You encompass everything in mercy and knowledge', the two appear together repeatedly.

outline.heading: Why scripture doesn't teach science
outline.gist: Answering an atheist's quip: science is a blessing, yet fewer died in all the Prophet's battles than in single incidents today.

outline.heading: Has science made us happier?
outline.gist: Technology has advanced but whether quality of life and purpose have improved depends on criteria we lack.

outline.heading: Science is a tool, not a goal
outline.gist: Without mercy any knowledge, scientific or religious, gets abused for personal gain.

outline.heading: Islamic knowledge can be twisted too
outline.gist: The highest potential for good, yet it can be bent to an agenda; knowledge alone in the package is a philosophical problem.

outline.heading: Military budgets and the nuclear era
outline.gist: Knowledge without mercy smashed a door that cannot be closed; scientific verses stay understandable in any era, like the sun's course.

outline.heading: Why do we send our children to university?
outline.gist: Learning for prestige is wasted years; increasing knowledge without guidance only increases distance from Allah.

outline.heading: Myths about al-Khidr
outline.gist: Claims that he is alive or a prophet are unfounded; he is one of Allah's servants and agents carrying knowledge and mercy.

outline.heading: Musa's request: 'May I follow you?'
outline.gist: No credentials, just the humble language of following, as we are asked to follow the Prophet.

outline.heading: Rushd: knowledge that works in reality
outline.gist: The same word as the cave youths' prayer; Musa knows the Torah and wants the practical wisdom to apply it.

outline.heading: Reacting just as Musa reacts
outline.gist: Musa was told the man acts on Allah's command, yet events would look unjust; reality differs from theory.

outline.heading: Counselling others versus doing it yourself
outline.gist: You advise a friend on marriage or parenting then do the same thing at home; Musa expected a lecture, not events.

outline.heading: 'You will not be able to be patient with me'
outline.gist: Speaking up when something seems wrong is fine; the teacher predicts Musa will not last.

outline.heading: Patience requires understanding the whole picture
outline.gist: Khubr and the name al-Muhit; no one can persevere with what they don't grasp, and Islam never asks blind acceptance.

outline.heading: True knowledge gives people the excuse
outline.gist: The teacher excused Musa in advance; teaching your child maths for four minutes shows why understanding the reason calms you.

outline.heading: A note on istata'a
outline.gist: The normal form of the verb here; the change in form later will be discussed then.

outline.heading: People who haven't bought in will leave
outline.gist: Employees or children not convinced will break eventually; after the Prophet's death, those who had not learned the faith turned back.

outline.heading: Understanding prevents anger
outline.gist: With knowledge and mercy you see the reason behind mistakes and stop yelling, hitting or pushing people away.

outline.heading: Raise awareness so youth can commit
outline.gist: You cannot expect chastity, hijab or a different campus lifestyle from youth who don't understand why.

outline.heading: 'You will find me patient, insha'Allah'
outline.gist: Musa, among the greatest of humans, promises patience and obedience to a man he just met.

outline.heading: One condition: ask me nothing
outline.gist: Don't ask until I mention it to you; interrupting is natural for someone without the full picture.

outline.heading: Outro

18:45.ar: وَٱضۡرِبۡ لَهُم مَّثَلَ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا كَمَآءٍ أَنزَلۡنَٰهُ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ فَٱخۡتَلَطَ بِهِۦ نَبَاتُ ٱلۡأَرۡضِ فَأَصۡبَحَ هَشِيمࣰ ا تَذۡرُوهُ ٱلرِّيَٰحُۗ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءࣲ مُّقۡتَدِرًا
18:45.en: And coin for them the similitude of the life of the world as water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingleth with it and then becometh dry twigs that the winds scatter. Allah is able to do all things

18:46.ar: ٱلۡمَالُ وَٱلۡبَنُونَ زِينَةُ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَاۖ وَٱلۡبَٰقِيَٰتُ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتُ خَيۡرٌ عِندَ رَبِّكَ ثَوَابࣰ ا وَخَيۡرٌ أَمَلࣰ ا
18:46.en: Wealth and children are an ornament of the life of the world. But the good deeds which endure are better in thy Lord's sight for reward, and better in respect of hope

18:47.ar: وَيَوۡمَ نُسَيِّرُ ٱلۡجِبَالَ وَتَرَى ٱلۡأَرۡضَ بَارِزَةࣰ وَحَشَرۡنَٰهُمۡ فَلَمۡ نُغَادِرۡ مِنۡهُمۡ أَحَدࣰ ا
18:47.en: And (bethink you of) the Day when we remove the hills and ye see the earth emerging, and We gather them together so as to leave not one of them behind

18:48.ar: وَعُرِضُواْ عَلَىٰ رَبِّكَ صَفࣰّ ا لَّقَدۡ جِئۡتُمُونَا كَمَا خَلَقۡنَٰكُمۡ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةِۭۚ بَلۡ زَعَمۡتُمۡ أَلَّن نَّجۡعَلَ لَكُم مَّوۡعِدࣰ ا
18:48.en: And they are set before thy Lord in ranks (and it is said unto them): Now verily have ye come unto Us as We created you at the first. But ye thought that We had set no tryst for you

7:32.ar: قُلۡ مَنۡ حَرَّمَ زِينَةَ ٱللَّهِ ٱلَّتِيٓ أَخۡرَجَ لِعِبَادِهِۦ وَٱلطَّيِّبَٰتِ مِنَ ٱلرِّزۡقِۚ قُلۡ هِيَ لِلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ فِي ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا خَالِصَةࣰ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِۗ كَذَٰلِكَ نُفَصِّلُ ٱلۡأٓيَٰتِ لِقَوۡمࣲ يَعۡلَمُونَ
7:32.en: Say: Who hath forbidden the adornment of Allah which He hath brought forth for His bondmen, and the good things of His providing? Say: Such, on the Day of Resurrection, will be only for those who believed during the life of the world. Thus do we detail Our revelations for people who have knowledge

2:30.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ رَبُّكَ لِلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ إِنِّي جَاعِلࣱ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ خَلِيفَةࣰۖ قَالُوٓاْ أَتَجۡعَلُ فِيهَا مَن يُفۡسِدُ فِيهَا وَيَسۡفِكُ ٱلدِّمَآءَ وَنَحۡنُ نُسَبِّحُ بِحَمۡدِكَ وَنُقَدِّسُ لَكَۖ قَالَ إِنِّيٓ أَعۡلَمُ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُونَ
2:30.en: And when thy Lord said unto the angels: Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth, they said: Wilt thou place therein one who will do harm therein and will shed blood, while we, we hymn Thy praise and sanctify Thee? He said: Surely I know that which ye know not

51:56.ar: وَمَا خَلَقۡتُ ٱلۡجِنَّ وَٱلۡإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعۡبُدُونِ
51:56.en: I created the jinn and humankind only that they might worship Me

18:35.ar: وَدَخَلَ جَنَّتَهُۥ وَهُوَ ظَالِمࣱ لِّنَفۡسِهِۦ قَالَ مَآ أَظُنُّ أَن تَبِيدَ هَٰذِهِۦٓ أَبَدࣰ ا
18:35.en: And he went into his garden, while he (thus) wronged himself. He said: I think not that all this will ever perish

18:36.ar: وَمَآ أَظُنُّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ قَآئِمَةࣰ وَلَئِن رُّدِدتُّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي لَأَجِدَنَّ خَيۡرࣰ ا مِّنۡهَا مُنقَلَبࣰ ا
18:36.en: I think not that the Hour will ever come, and if indeed I am brought back unto my Lord I surely shall find better than this as a resort
